Class OidcAuthorizeEndpoint

java.lang.Object
iu.oidc.provider.OidcAuthorizeEndpoint
public class OidcAuthorizeEndpoint extends Object
Answers the OpenID Connect authorization request.

Only the authorization code flow. Nothing here is a servlet, and nothing here knows how the end user authenticates: it takes a request, reports what came of it, and leaves both the transport and the identity provider to whatever called it.

Two passes

A request arrives carrying client_id. The endpoint validates it, records the validated request as an OidcGrant in a session of its own, and — when no principal is established yet — answers OidcAuthorizeResult.AuthenticationRequired, naming the bare authorization endpoint as where the end user comes back to.

That second pass carries no client_id, which is what marks it as a resumption: the request is read back out of the session rather than off the query string, so state, nonce, and the PKCE challenge never travel through the identity provider or turn up in its logs. A request that already has a principal skips the round trip and issues a code on the first pass.

The principal arrives as a Supplier rather than a value, so it is looked up only once the request is worth looking one up for — a request naming an unregistered client is refused without ever asking who the end user is.

Granted scope

A client registers endpoints, each keyed by its redirect URI, and each endpoint declares the resources it may act on. The requested redirect_uri selects the endpoint; the requested resource — which RFC 8707 permits naming more than once, for a token meant to be usable at several resources at once — selects among that endpoint's resources, or, when the request names none, every resource whose scope overlaps what was asked for. An entry registered without a URI names this provider's own issuer identifier, so a request naming the issuer itself matches it too; that is what lets a deployment grant a token addressed to itself — openid, say — without the registration embedding its own issuer URI, which would tie it to one deployment. The scopes those resources declare are everything the request may ask for; openid is not a special case beyond that.

What is named here is recorded on the grant, not merely checked and discarded: a token endpoint bounds the audience of a token redeemed against this authorization — directly or through a refresh token descending from it — to at most these resources, however the redemption request's own resource parameter reads.

Errors

Follows OAuth 2.0: once client_id and redirect_uri check out, an invalid request answers a OidcAuthorizeResult.Redirect to the client carrying error and error_description. Before that point there is no verified URI to redirect to, so the endpoint raises IuBadRequestException and the caller answers the user agent where it stands — redirecting an error to an unverified URI would make this an open redirector.

    • OidcAuthorizeEndpoint

      public OidcAuthorizeEndpoint(OidcIssuer issuer, edu.iu.oidc.config.OidcClientSource clients, edu.iu.session.IuSessionHandler sessionHandler, GrantStore grantStore)
      Creates an authorization endpoint.
      Parameters:
      issuer - this provider's own identity and signing keys
      clients - reads a relying party's registration
      sessionHandler - holds the validated request across the round trip to the identity provider; must be a handler of its own, since a handler shared with the authentication mechanism would have each overwrite the other's cookie
      grantStore - hands the completed grant to the token endpoint

  • Method Details

    • authorize

      public OidcAuthorizeResult authorize(OidcAuthorizeRequest request, Supplier<edu.iu.oidc.config.OidcAuthenticatedPrincipal> principal)
      Answers an authorization request, or resumes one the identity provider has returned from.
      Parameters:
      request - incoming request
      principal - supplies the principal the identity provider has established, answering null when it has established none. The supplier itself is required; it is the value it supplies that may be absent, which is the ordinary first pass rather than a failure. Consulted at most once, and only once a request is worth consulting it for
      Returns:
      what the request came to
      Throws:
      edu.iu.IuBadRequestException - if the request names no verified client and redirect URI to relay an error to
      NullPointerException - if principal is null
